title: Study: one knight, two files
author: Christer Jonsson
source: Springaren 1998, Swedish national tourney, 3rd Prize (Problemesis record psis-4d1711af7b)
teaser: A study post: today's own attempts did not reach a sound problem, so here is a prize-winner that does what they tried to do. Twelve units, no flight. The black knight a2 stands on one White rook's file and can jump onto the other's. Look at what each queen mate needs from the two rooks, and at which White piece leaves which square.

comment.what: A study post. Today's searches and hand constructions found no sound original (see How it was made), so the skill's fallback applies: an archive problem of the theme, with full credit. Jonsson's 3rd Prize shows Le Grand with no flight at all: the try threatens 2.Qa5# and after 1...Sc3 mates by 2.Qa6#; the key threatens 2.Qa6# and after the same 1...Sc3 mates by 2.Qa5#. The defence does two things at once. The knight leaves a2, so the rook a1 now protects a5 and a6; and it lands on c3, so the rook c2 no longer guards c5, c6 and c7. In the try the knight has gone from d8 to b7 and the bishop still stands on c6, protected only along the c-file: after 1...Sc3 the king could take it, so 2.Qa5# fails, and 2.Qa6#, protected by Ra1, mates: the queen covers c6 through the king along the sixth rank, and the knight b7 covers c5. In the key the bishop has gone from c6 to b7 and protects a6; after 1...Sc3 the square c5 has lost its only guard, so 2.Qa6# fails, and 2.Qa5#, protected by Ra1 and covering c5 along the fifth rank, mates. Our solver confirms the published solution and reports the Le Grand on 1...Sc3 between 1.Sb7? and 1.Bb7!, and a Dombrovskis effect with 1.Bb5?.
flaws: The try 1.Sb7? is refuted by a capture of the bishop, 1...Sxc6!, which is not a thematic defence.
Thin play after the key: only 1...Sc3 has its own mate; the other knight moves (Sc8, Sc6, Sb5) allow both the threat and 2.Rc6#, a by-play dual that the published solution leaves out.
The White king h1 takes no part, and the pawn d6 is needed in no mate of the solution (the anatomy's removal test): it guards c7, a square the queen's mates also cover, and is there for soundness.
In the diagram 1...Sc3 already has two mates (2.Qxa7# and 2.Qa5#), so the set play shows no clean third answer.
This is not our work: it is published as a study, credited to its author, because today's original failed.
pluses: Le Grand without a flight: the defence is a line switch by one black unit (open one White file, close the other), not a king move. Our own attempts all hung on a flight and its guards; this mechanism needs none.
Two tries on the same pair of mates, with a Dombrovskis effect: 1.Bb5? threatens 2.Qa6# like the key and is refuted by the thematic defence 1...Sc3!, which after the key is answered.
The try and the key land on the same square, b7, by different units: which unit leaves which square (d8 or c6) decides which of c5/c6 the closed c-file still matters for.
Light: 7+5, a quiet key that leaves the bishop's guard of b5 to the queen.
comment.process: Theme from the rotation: Le Grand, a stretch theme with no reference in the kit. About 45 minutes by the container clock (it runs slow against the work done), about 60 solves and try tables, 24 search jobs. (1) evolve with PATTERN='Le Grand' on four bare cores: one position a second, nothing in 40 job-minutes. (2) A new fast scorer (chesscomp.compose.legrand: python-chess only, mates looked for among checking moves) at about 30 positions a second; its hill climb drifted away from every seed, including good ones, and found no HIT in 16 runs. (3) By hand, the cross-geometry of the archive's flight Le Grands (Bourd, Labai) on a new square: Ke4, flight d5, the queen a6 mating on c4 or d3. The problem was the extra square: whatever the try adds (e3 or f3) is a diagram flight. (4) A hinge instead of a square: a black bishop g1 interposing on d4 against both distant checks, cut by a White unit landing on e3. The exhaustive pair layer (every one or two added units, about 100 seconds) found the pair at once: 1.Be3? (2.Qc4#) Kd5 2.Qd3# and 1.Be2? (2.Qd3#) Kd5 2.Qc4#, a Le Grand, but both are tries. The hinge refutes them both: 1...Bxe3! takes the interferer and still reaches d4, and 1...Bd4! blocks d4 in advance and closes the d-file, which carried the guard of the flight. Three more layers of added units did not find a key. See the attempts below.
comment.lesson: A black line piece used as a hinge (an interposer that the try or key cuts off) has two moves of its own that the scheme must survive: it can occupy the interposition square in advance, and it can capture the cutting unit and interpose from there. In today's scheme the first closed the guard line of the flight and the second came back to d4, so the Le Grand stayed between two tries. Check both before building around a hinge, or choose a defence that switches lines (Jonsson: one knight opens one White file and closes another), which has no such side-moves.

attempts.title: Le Grand between two tries, no key (the hinge on g1)
attempts.note: 1.Be3? (2.Qc4#) 1...Kd5 2.Qd3#, but 1...Bxe3!; 1.Be2? (2.Qd3#) 1...Kd5 2.Qc4#, but 1...Bd4!. The bishop e3 cuts the black bishop g1 off d4, where it would interpose against both distant checks. Gate: FAIL, no solution. The hinge refutes both tries by its own moves (capture of the interferer, self-block on d4).

attempts.title: The first kernel: duals after the flight
attempts.note: 1.Kf2? (2.Qc4#) but 1...g3+!; 1.Be2! (2.Qd3#) 1...Kd5 2.Qc4#, but also 2.Qd3#, Qc6#, Qb7#, Qa8#, and the checks 1.Qc4+, 1.Qe2+, 1.Bc2+ solve too (cooked). The queen on a6 sees the long diagonal and the sixth rank, so the flight d5 has five mates.

mentor_questions: Today's best attempt has the Le Grand between two tries (1.Be3? and 1.Be2?, each refuted by a move of the black hinge bishop) and no key. If a key with its own threat were found, would a Le Grand between two tries count as the theme for you, or must the key carry one of the two threats?

The light archive Le Grands by flight (Labai, and your Problemesis 2005 problem) have the flight in the diagram, and in yours it has no set mate. Our gate calls an unprovided diagram flight fatal. When the flight IS the Le Grand defence, is it acceptable to you, or should the flight be provided or given by the key?
improvement: A Le Grand kit, the theme's first. python -m chesscomp.compose.legrand scores a position for the theme in a few milliseconds with python-chess alone (an ordered pair of quiet first moves with single different threats and a Black move that swaps them, then the key's soundness and uniqueness, the try's refutations, diagram flights and their set mates); evolve's solver-based score ran at one position a second. Its 'pairs' mode adds every one or two units around a hand kernel and found today's Le Grand pair in 100 seconds, where the hill climb found nothing. Fixed during the run: mates are compared by piece and arrival square (Qh5-f5 and Qf1-f5 are the same mate), and a seed king on a1 (square 0) is no longer taken for a missing king. Tested in tests/test_legrand.py (Labai's problem is a HIT, Bourd's unprovided flight is not, the pairs layer finds today's pair). The new reference .claude/skills/themes/references/le_grand.md has the four engines in the archive, the flight problem, and the hinge trap; blog/themes.json points to it.
